extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of political theory and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria and normative observations for evaluating federal systems, political parties, and the liberty of the press, illustrated by the United States example. Useful for comparative-political assessment of institutional durability, party dynamics, and press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness of political propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition must be plain to be adopted by the understanding of a people; a false notion which is clear and precise will always meet with a greater number of adherents than a true principle which is obscure or involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, easily defined principles and names become symbols that parties and communities adopt and act upon; governments 'founded upon a single principle or a single feeling which is easily defined' are often the strongest and most durable, even if not the best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional systems presuppose civic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution of the United States presupposes a variety of information and the excellence of discretion in the people whom it is meant to govern; the government of the Union depends entirely upon legal fictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal constitutions work better where the populace is accustomed to conduct its own affairs and where political knowledge 'has descended to the humblest classes'; copying a constitution without the civic spirit leads to dysfunction (example: Mexico).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided sovereignty weakens central government
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle upon which all confederations rest is that of a divided sovereignty... a divided sovereignty must always be less powerful than an entire supremacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators can conceal or soften partitions of power but cannot eliminate the fundamental weakness created by divided sovereignty; this is an inherent defect of federal/confederate systems compared to centralized states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal-state conflict can produce collective resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Federal law were to clash with the interests and the prejudices of a State, all the citizens of that State might unite in a common defence against the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When federal authority injures a state's perceived core interests, individual enforcement may fail because citizens organize around shared state-level grievances; legal fictions (e.g., litigating in names of purchasers rather than states) may collapse into reality and produce organized opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability of confederations requires shared inducements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal compact cannot be lasting unless there exists in the communities which are leagued together a certain number of inducements to union which render their common dependence agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful federations rest on common interests, a common origin and tongue, and a similar stage of civilization; geographical position and uniformity of manners/customs also contribute to feasibility (contrast: Switzerland's cantonal differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of civilization necessary for federation success
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain uniformity of civilization is not less necessary to the durability of a confederation than a uniformity of interests in the States which compose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large differences in civilization or historical development among constituent units may render federal government impracticable because a central authority cannot impose uniform laws on disparate populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: War tends to strengthen governments and expose federal weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: All the peoples which have been obliged to sustain a long and serious warfare have consequently been led to augment the power of their government... A long war almost always places nations in the wretched alternative of being abandoned to ruin by defeat or to despotism by success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal systems are particularly vulnerable because their divided sovereignty and imperfect central administration make coordinated wartime action difficult; war therefore reveals and exacerbates federal weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central organization and command deficits reduce federal efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal system is not only deficient in every kind of centralized administration, but the central government itself is imperfectly organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical problems—like disputes over militia command (example from War of 1812 where states refused federal orders)—illustrate that unclear command structures and reserved state prerogatives hamper federal capacity in crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic insulation mitigates external threats
rubrics_metrics.description: The only safeguard which the American Union... possesses against the dissolution which would be produced by a great war, lies in its probable exemption from that calamity... Placed in the centre of an immense continent... the Union is almost as much insulated from the world as if its frontiers were girt by the ocean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geography (vast territory, weak neighbors, sparse population in bordering regions) can compensate for institutional weaknesses by reducing likelihood of large-scale foreign wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular sovereignty exercised through frequent direct elections
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the people appoints the legislative and the executive power, and furnishes the jurors who punish all offences against the laws... the people elects its representatives directly, and for the most part annually, in order to ensure their dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative institutions in the US are highly democratic in practice because of direct and frequent electoral accountability, making public opinion and majority rule the real directing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule and pervasiveness of parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority governs in the name of the people... the opinions, the prejudices, the interests, and even the passions of the community are hindered by no durable obstacles from exercising a perpetual influence on society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are the instruments through which majorities aggregate opinion; constant party activity and agitation shape governance in a democracy where representatives depend on popular support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between great and minor parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The political parties which I style great are those which cling to principles more than to their consequences... Minor parties are, on the other hand, generally deficient in political faith... they glow with a factitious zeal; their language is vehement, but their conduct is timid and irresolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great parties emphasize enduring ideas and public-spirited convictions; minor parties focus on private interest, display ostentatious rhetoric but lack coherent, courageous action; the two have different effects on society (great tear it, minor degrade it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty and method of creating parties in the US
rubrics_metrics.description: The pains which are taken to create parties are inconceivable... A political aspirant in the United States begins by discriminating his own interest, and by calculating upon those interests which may be collected around and amalgamated with it; he then contrives to discover some doctrine or some principle which may suit the purposes of this new association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the usual social cleavages (religion, rank, poverty) are weak or absent, parties are often artificially constructed by ambitious individuals who seek doctrines to rally disparate interests into a political association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying aristocratic or democratic impulses in all parties
rubrics_metrics.description: I affirm that aristocratic or democratic passions may easily be detected at the bottom of all parties... the object of the one is to limit, and that of the other to extend, the popular authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when not explicit, parties tend to embody tendencies either to concentrate power (aristocratic) or to expand popular rule (democratic); recognizing these latent tendencies helps explain party behavior and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of the wealthy elite in democratic societies
rubrics_metrics.description: The wealthy members of the community abandon the lists, through unwillingness to contend... They concentrate all their enjoyments in the privacy of their homes... They submit to this state of things as an irremediable evil, but they are careful not to show that they are galled by its continuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affluent citizens may retreat from public life, mask their wealth publicly, form exclusive private societies, and affect condescension toward the people—practices that preserve social distinction while avoiding direct political contestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal instruments of party success: press and associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The two chief weapons which parties use in order to ensure success are the public press and the formation of associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties rely on periodical press to shape opinion and on organized associations to mobilize support; these are central mechanisms of modern political contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press is hard to regulate without effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of the liberty of the press does not affect political opinions alone... If you proceed [to repress abuses] you must bring the delinquent before a court of permanent judges. But even here the cause must be heard before it can be decided; and the very principles which no book would have ventured to avow are blazoned forth in the pleadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to restrain press abuses via prosecution are fraught: jury trials may convert individual opinions into widespread ones (acquittal), while judicial trials publicize controversial principles through legal pleadings. Finding an intermediate, tenable position between complete independence and entire subjection is very difficult.
